blocks.text:
### How to use this guide

- **Read it in order the first time.** The opening parts build the mental model (what Kafka is and how it works inside), then come the plain Java clients, schemas and Spring Boot, followed by Kafka Streams, Kafka Connect and the design patterns. Use the contents page to jump to what you need. This edition does not yet include the hands-on installation labs, the consumer API chapters, the use-case catalogue, the end-to-end projects, the operations part or the interview kit.
- **Every chapter follows the same rhythm:** what it is, why it exists, how it works, how to implement it (with code), what goes wrong, and a short key-points box. Coloured boxes mean: NOTE (extra detail), TIP (practical advice), WATCH OUT and GOTCHA (mistakes that cost people days), REAL WORLD (how it appears in production), INTERVIEW ANGLE (what interviewers like to ask).
- **Labs are hands-on.** A dark box is a terminal session: lines beginning with `$` are what you type, the other lines are the output you should see. Output is shown as typical output; IDs, timestamps and offsets on your machine will differ.
- **About the code.** Every code listing was written against the official documentation for the versions named on the cover and checked for syntax. They were not executed against a live broker while this guide was produced, so treat the first run on your machine as part of the lab: if a command or listing behaves differently, the official docs for your exact version are the final word.
- **Running example.** Most examples use one fictional online shop, *ShopStream*, with orders, payments, inventory and notifications. Seeing the same domain across chapters lets you focus on Kafka, not on the business problem.
- **Conventions.** `monospace` is code, a command or a configuration name. Configuration defaults quoted in this guide are those of Kafka 4.2 documentation unless stated. Topic names use lowercase with dots or hyphens.

sections.title: The Problem Kafka Was Built to Solve

blocks.text:
Imagine you are building ShopStream, an online shop. When a customer clicks **Place order**, a surprising amount of work has to happen. The card must be charged. Stock must be reserved. A confirmation email should go out. The warehouse needs a shipment to pack. The analytics team wants the sale on their dashboard, and the search page should learn which products are selling fast. ShopStream is the running example for this whole book, so it is worth spending a few minutes on how this work should be organised. That question is the reason Kafka exists.

### The direct-call design and its tangle

The design most teams reach for first is the direct one. `order-service` saves the order and then calls every other system in turn, usually over HTTP.

blocks.title: OrderService.java (the direct-call design, simplified)

blocks.text:
This works on day one and hurts on day ninety. Look at what `order-service` has to know, and what it has to put up with.

- **It knows every consumer of its data.** Each call hard-codes an address, an API and a payload format. A new interested system, say a fraud checker, means changing and redeploying `order-service`.
- **Everyone must be awake right now.** If the email service is down, either the order fails or you write retry and fallback code for every single call.
- **The slowest callee sets the pace.** The customer waits while the analytics call finishes, although the customer does not care about analytics.
- **The problem multiplies.** `order-service` is only one producer of facts. `payment-service` has facts that others need (a payment was authorised), and so do inventory, shipping and the web front end.

If N systems produce data and M systems need it, point-to-point wiring needs up to N × M integrations. Each one has its own protocol, data format, error handling, monitoring and owner. Ten producers and fifteen consumers can mean as many as 150 connections to build and keep alive (an illustrative number, but real systems get there faster than anyone plans).

blocks.text:
### Batch versus real time

The other classic answer is the **batch job**. Once a night a script extracts yesterday's data from the order database, transforms it, and loads it into a warehouse, a search index and a reporting database. This pattern is called ETL (extract, transform, load). Batch processing is simple, robust and very efficient for large volumes, and it is still the right tool for many jobs, such as monthly revenue reports.

Its weakness is **staleness**: the data is exactly as old as the last run. Some questions can wait until tomorrow. Others cannot. Is this card payment fraudulent? Is the last pair of size-42 red shoes about to sell out? Which products should the home page promote right now? The value of this kind of information decays quickly with age.

Batch extraction also tends to hit the application database directly, which adds load to a system that is busy serving customers, and it couples every job to the internal table layout of the source system.

"Real time" in this book does not mean microseconds. It means reacting within seconds, or less, **as events happen**, instead of hours later. What we want is a way to move facts between systems continuously, reliably and without every pair of systems having to know about each other.

### The shared log in the middle

The idea behind Kafka is to put one durable, ordered, append-only **log** in the middle. A producer does not call anybody. It appends an event describing what happened to the log. Consumers read the log at their own pace, and each consumer keeps its own bookmark that says how far it has read.

Think of a shared notebook in the office. Anyone can write a new line at the bottom, nobody erases lines, and every reader keeps a bookmark at the last line they read. A reader on holiday does not stop anybody else from writing; when they return they simply continue from their bookmark. That picture is surprisingly close to how Kafka behaves, and the "bookmark" will come back as the **offset** in the next chapters.

Here is what this buys ShopStream:

- **Decoupling in space.** `order-service` publishes `OrderCreated` once. It does not know, and does not need to know, who reads it.
- **Decoupling in time.** If `notification-service` is down for an hour, events wait in the log. When the service comes back, it continues from its bookmark. Nothing is lost and nobody else noticed.
- **Decoupling in speed.** A slow consumer slows only itself. The producer and the other consumers carry on.
- **History and replay.** A new consumer can start from the beginning of the log. If you find a bug in your analytics code, you fix it, move the bookmark back, and process the history again.
- **One agreed order.** All consumers see the same events in the same order, so their copies of the truth do not drift apart for ordering reasons.

Six months later the data science team wants fraud scoring. In the direct design they must negotiate with the `order-service` team, wait for a new release, and accept that the new HTTP call slows every checkout. In the log design they write a consumer, start it at the oldest event and let it catch up. The `order-service` code does not change at all.

Why a *log* and not just a clever queue? Appending to the end of a file and reading it sequentially is what disks, operating systems and CPU caches do best. An append-only structure is also easy to replicate: followers copy the leader's log in the same order. The architecture part of this book shows how much of Kafka's performance and reliability comes from this one design choice.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: A log in the middle is not free. You now operate (or pay for) a distributed system. Consumers see data slightly later than the producer wrote it, so the system is **eventually consistent**: the confirmation email may go out a second after the order. Events become a public contract, and changing their shape can break readers you have never met. Debugging a flow means following an event across several services instead of reading one stack trace. And delivery is normally *at* *least once*, so consumers must cope with seeing the same event twice. Later parts show how to handle each of these.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why put a broker such as Kafka between services instead of calling them directly? Because it decouples producers from consumers in space (they do not know each other), in time (a consumer can be down and catch up later) and in speed (a slow consumer does not slow the producer). It also turns N x M point-to-point integrations into N + M, and new consumers can be added years later without touching the producer. Direct calls remain the right tool when the caller needs an answer right now, for example to validate a card before confirming an order.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- Point-to-point integration needs up to N × M connections and couples systems in code, in time and in speed.
- Batch jobs are simple and efficient, but the data they deliver is as old as the last run.
- Kafka puts a durable, ordered, append-only log in the middle: producers append, consumers read at their own pace and keep their own bookmark.
- The log gives decoupling, replay and one agreed order, at the price of running a distributed system and of eventual consistency.

sections.title: What Kafka Is (and What It Is Not)

blocks.text:
Apache Kafka is an open-source, distributed **event streaming platform**. That phrase is dense, so this chapter unpacks it: what an event is, what "streaming" adds, and what you get when you run a Kafka cluster. The official introduction calls event streaming "the digital equivalent of the human body's central nervous system". Things happen at the edges of your business (a click, a payment, a sensor reading), signals travel along the nerves, and the right parts of the organisation react immediately.

### Events

An **event** records the fact that something happened: a customer placed order `o-1001`, a payment was authorised, a visitor viewed a page. An event usually carries a description of what happened (the *value*), often something that says what it is about (the *key*, such as the order id), and a *timestamp*. Kafka's documentation uses the words event, record and message interchangeably. This book says **event** when it talks about the business meaning, and **record** when it talks about what Kafka stores and about the Java API (`ProducerRecord`, `ConsumerRecord`).

Two properties of events matter. First, they are *facts about the past*, so they are not edited. If an order is cancelled, you append an `OrderCancelled` event; you do not rewrite `OrderCreated`. Second, their *order* is information: it matters that the payment was authorised after the order was created. A structure that keeps events in order and never changes them is a log, and the log is the data structure Kafka is built around.

### The three capabilities

Kafka's documentation names three key capabilities of an event streaming platform. They also make a handy map of this book.

1. **Publish and subscribe.** Write streams of events into Kafka and read them out again, including the continuous import and export of data from and to other systems.
2. **Store.** Keep streams of events durably and reliably for as long as you want. Records are written to disk and copied to several servers. "As long as you want" is a policy that you set per topic: a number of days, a size, or forever.
3. **Process.** Work on streams of events as they occur, or retrospectively by reading history again.

blocks.text:
### Servers and clients

Kafka is a distributed system made of **servers** and **clients** that talk to each other over a binary protocol on top of TCP. The servers run as a cluster of one or more machines, and the documentation notes that a cluster can span several data centres or cloud regions. Some servers form the storage layer and are called **brokers**. Others run Kafka Connect to move data in and out of external systems. Your own applications are the clients: they use a client library to write events to the brokers (producers), read them (consumers), or process them.

The Apache Kafka project ships these Java APIs: the Producer API, the Consumer API, the Admin API (to manage and inspect topics, brokers and other objects), the Kafka Streams API for stream processing, and the Kafka Connect API for reusable import and export connectors. Client libraries for many other languages exist as well, and because the wire protocol is documented, anybody can write one.

### A durable, replicated log

This is the mental model to carry through the book. A topic is a named stream of records. Inside Kafka, the records of a topic are written to **append-only logs** on disk, and every log is replicated to other servers. Four rules follow.

- Records are only ever *appended* at the end, and an existing record is never modified.
- Every record gets a position in its log, the **offset**, which only grows.
- **Reading does not delete.** A consumer remembers a position and moves it forward. Many consumers can read the same record independently, and a new one can start from the beginning.
- Records leave the log only by policy: **retention** removes records that are older than a configured age (seven days by default) or when the log gets too large, and **compaction** can keep just the latest record per key.

Everything else in this book, from consumer groups to transactions, is built on these four rules.

### What Kafka is not

Being clear about the limits saves projects. Kafka is not the right tool for the following jobs, although you can find people who have tried all of them.

- **Not a replacement for your database.** Kafka stores history, but you cannot ask it "give me all customers in Pune with tier GOLD". There are no ad hoc queries and no secondary indexes. Kafka tells you what *happened*; a database tells you what is *true now* and lets you query it. Compacted topics and Kafka Streams state stores give you key lookups on the latest value, which is useful, but it is not a general query engine.
- **Not an RPC layer.** When a caller needs an answer right now (is this card valid?), use HTTP or gRPC. Request and reply over Kafka is possible (a pattern covered later) but adds latency and complexity.
- **Not a task scheduler.** Classic Kafka consumer groups have no delayed delivery, no priorities, no per-message timeouts. The newer share groups add queue-like per-record acknowledgement and redelivery, but not priorities or scheduled delivery.
- **Not a file or blob store.** The default maximum record size is about 1 MiB. Put large files in object storage and send a reference through Kafka (the claim-check pattern, covered in the design patterns part).
- **Not magic.** Kafka does not give you exactly-once effects in external systems, schema discipline, or free operations. It gives you a very good log; the rest is engineering.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Database engineers know this structure as a *commit log* or write-ahead log: every change is written to the end of a log first, and tables are just a convenient view of the log. Kafka makes that internal database structure a shared, replicated service for the whole organisation. That is why the Kafka documentation lists "Commit Log" among its use cases.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is Apache Kafka? A distributed, fault-tolerant event streaming platform. Producers append records to topics, which are split into partitions stored as replicated, append-only logs on a cluster of brokers; consumers read the records independently at their own pace. Records are retained by policy rather than deleted on read, so data can be replayed and processed as it arrives or later.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- An event is an immutable fact about something that happened; Kafka stores events as records in ordered, replicated, append-only logs.
- The three capabilities are publish and subscribe, durable storage, and stream processing.
- Reading never deletes. Consumers keep their own position, and retention or compaction decides what leaves the log.
- Kafka complements databases, RPC and job schedulers. It does not replace them.

1. `order-service` saves the order in its own database and builds an `OrderCreated` event. It hands the event to a **producer**, the Kafka client library running inside the service.
2. The event is addressed to a **topic** named `orders`. The producer sets the order id `o-1001` as the record's **key**.
3. The producer knows the addresses of a few **brokers** (the `bootstrap.servers` setting). It asks one of them for the cluster's metadata: which **partitions** does `orders` have, and which broker is the **leader** of each? It hashes the key to choose a partition, say partition 2, and sends the **record** to the broker that leads it.
4. The leader appends the record to the end of that partition's log. The record receives the next **offset**, say 41. Two **follower** replicas on other brokers copy it. With `acks=all` the leader reports success to the producer only after every in-sync replica has the record.
5. `payment-service` runs several instances that all use the group id `payment-service`. Together they form one **consumer group**, and Kafka gives each partition of `orders` to exactly one instance of the group. The instance that owns partition 2 **polls**, receives offset 41, charges the card, and **commits** offset 42 ("the next record I want"). The commit is stored in Kafka itself.
6. `inventory-service`, `notification-service` and `analytics-app` each have their own group. They read the same record independently, each at its own pace and with its own committed offsets. Nobody removes the record; it stays for the retention period (seven days by default).

What to notice: the producer talks directly to the broker that leads the partition, the key keeps all events of one order in one partition and therefore in order, and the services that read `orders` know nothing about each other.

### Topics and partitions

A **topic** is a named stream of records: the thing you publish to and subscribe to. ShopStream uses topics such as `orders`, `payments` and `page-views`. Kafka's documentation compares a topic to a folder in a filesystem, with the events as the files in that folder. A topic is a logical name, not one file. Kafka splits every topic into one or more **partitions**, and each partition is an ordered, append-only log that is stored on one broker and copied to others.

Why split? One log on one machine would limit a topic to what that machine can store and serve, and only one consumer could read it at a time. Spreading partitions over many brokers lets a topic grow beyond a single machine, and lets many consumers read different partitions in parallel.

Which partition does a record go to? If the record has a key, the producer hashes the key, so records with the same key always land in the same partition. If there is no key, the producer spreads records across partitions. Kafka guarantees order only **within a partition**, which is why `orders` uses `orderId` as its key: every event of order `o-1001` stays in the order in which it was written.

blocks.text:
### Offsets: a bookmark in the log

Inside a partition every record receives an **offset**, a sequential number that starts at 0 and only grows. The offset is the record's address and the consumer's bookmark. A consumer that has processed up to offset 41 will ask for offset 42 next; a new consumer may start at offset 0 and read the whole history; a consumer that crashed can resume where it left off.

blocks.text:
The triple (topic, partition, offset) identifies one record uniquely. Offsets belong to a partition, and they are never reused, so "offset 41" means nothing until you say in which partition. A consumer keeps two related numbers for each partition: its **position**, the offset of the next record it will receive, and its **committed offset**, the last position it saved in Kafka so that it can resume after a restart. The chapters on the Java consumer explain the difference in detail.

### Consumer groups

A **consumer group** is a set of consumers that share one `group.id` and cooperate to read a topic. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group at a time. If `orders` has three partitions and `payment-service` runs three instances, each instance reads one partition. If one instance crashes, Kafka moves its partition to a survivor, which is called a **rebalance**.

Two consequences are worth remembering now. A group can use at most as many consumers as the topic has partitions; extra consumers sit idle as standbys. And different groups are completely independent: each group gets every record and keeps its own offsets. This single design gives Kafka both classic messaging models, as the next chapter shows.

### Brokers, clusters and replication

A **broker** is a Kafka server process that stores partitions on disk and serves producers and consumers. Several brokers form a **cluster**. Every partition has a configurable number of copies, the **replication factor**. One copy is the **leader**, which handles the writes, and the others are **followers** that continuously fetch from the leader and append the same records in the same order. Followers that keep up form the **in-sync replica set** (ISR). If the broker holding a leader fails, the cluster promotes an in-sync follower to be the new leader and clients carry on. A replication factor of 3, meaning three copies of your data, is the usual production choice.

Someone also has to keep track of cluster metadata: which topics exist, where the leaders are, what the settings are. Since Kafka 4.0 Kafka does this itself with a protocol called **KRaft**. A small group of **controller** nodes, often three, keeps the metadata in a replicated log, and brokers read from it. Older Kafka versions needed a separate ZooKeeper cluster for this. The architecture part of this book explains KRaft and replication in depth.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Offsets are per partition, not per topic. There is no global sequence number across the partitions of a topic. Offset 41 exists once in every partition. This is also why Kafka cannot tell you which of two records in different partitions was "first" except by comparing timestamps, and why ordering requirements must be translated into key choices.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do consumer groups give Kafka both queue and publish-subscribe behaviour? Within one group each partition is read by exactly one consumer, so the group's members share the work like competing consumers on a queue. Each group, however, receives every record independently, like a separate subscriber in publish-subscribe. One topic can therefore feed a scalable worker pool and several unrelated applications at once.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- A producer appends records to a topic. The topic is split into partitions, and each partition is an ordered log in which every record has an offset.
- The key decides the partition, so records with the same key stay together and in order. Order exists only within a partition.
- A consumer group shares a topic's partitions between its members; different groups read independently and keep their own committed offsets.
- Each partition is replicated on several brokers: one leader takes the writes, followers copy it, and a follower takes over if the leader fails.

No tool is best at everything. This chapter places Kafka among the tools it is usually compared with, in design discussions and in interviews. The comparisons are conceptual and avoid performance numbers on purpose: results depend on workload, configuration and hardware, and products change quickly. Always check a product's current documentation and licence before you decide.

### Two classic models and Kafka's hybrid

Messaging systems traditionally offer one of two models. In a **queue**, many consumers compete for messages and each message is processed by exactly one of them, which is ideal for sharing work but means a second application cannot see the same message. In **publish-subscribe**, every subscriber receives every message, which is ideal for broadcasting but gives you no way to share the work inside one subscriber. Kafka's consumer groups combine both: competing consumers inside a group, broadcast between groups.

### Traditional message brokers

Classic brokers such as RabbitMQ and Apache ActiveMQ are built around queues. A producer sends a message, the broker routes it into one or more queues, delivers it to a consumer, waits for an acknowledgement and then deletes the message. The broker tracks the state of every message. Kafka inverts this: the broker stores an ordered log and does not care who has read it, while each consumer group tracks its own position and pulls the records it wants.

blocks.text:
Be fair to both sides. Brokers excel at flexible routing, per-message TTLs, priorities and request-reply at moderate volume. RabbitMQ has also added a stream type that is a replayable append-only log, which shows how useful the log idea is. Kafka, on the other hand, now offers share groups, which give queue-style consumption of a topic with per-record acknowledgement. The two worlds are moving closer, but their defaults and strengths still differ.

### Kafka and databases

A database stores the **current state** of your data and lets you query it in flexible ways. Kafka stores the **history of** **changes** and lets you read it in order. The two fit together more often than they compete.

- You can rebuild state by replaying a log of changes, and a table is just the latest value for each key in a stream of changes. This stream-table duality is the foundation of Kafka Streams and of compacted topics.
- A database answers "which customers in Pune are GOLD tier?" with an index. Kafka can only read by topic, partition and offset (or find an offset for a timestamp). Anything richer needs a consumer that builds a view of the data.
- The common production pattern is a database as the system of record and Kafka as the way changes leave it, using change data capture or the outbox pattern, both covered later. Some teams go further and treat the log as the system of record (event sourcing), accepting that every query then needs a projection.

### Managed cloud messaging services

Every large cloud offers managed messaging. In outline: Amazon SQS is a managed queue, Amazon SNS fans notifications out to subscribers, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a managed partitioned stream, Google Cloud Pub/Sub is a managed publish-subscribe service with per-subscription acknowledgements, and Azure Event Hubs is a managed partitioned log. Microsoft's own documentation calls Kafka and Event Hubs "very similar", since both are partitioned logs where the client chooses which part of the retained log to read, and Event Hubs exposes a Kafka endpoint so that existing Kafka clients can connect after a configuration change. The same page lists limitations, so test your own workload.

The trade-off is usually the same. A managed service removes cluster operations and fits neatly into one cloud, but it ties you to that provider's API, limits and pricing. Kafka is an open protocol with many implementations and vendors, runs on your laptop as easily as in any cloud, and has the broader ecosystem of connectors and stream processing. For a small team that lives in one cloud and has modest needs, the native service can be the better choice.

### Pulsar and Redpanda

**Apache Pulsar** is a separate Apache project with a different architecture. Its brokers are stateless, and messages are stored by Apache BookKeeper, a distributed log storage system, so serving and storage can scale separately. Geo-replication and tenant namespaces are part of its design, and it offers several subscription types, including queue-like shared subscriptions. The price is more moving parts to run (brokers, BookKeeper nodes and a metadata store) and a smaller surrounding ecosystem than Kafka's.

**Redpanda** is a Kafka-API-compatible streaming platform implemented in C++, so it runs without a JVM. Existing Kafka clients and many tools can talk to it. Compatibility is a strength, but it is never a guarantee of identical behaviour in every corner (transactions, administration, newer protocol features), so test with your own clients and check the licence terms. The same caution applies to every other system that speaks the Kafka protocol.

### When to use Kafka, and when not to

Kafka is a strong choice when:

- Many systems need the same stream of events, and new consumers will appear over time.
- You need to replay history, or let consumers fall behind and catch up later.
- Volume is high or growing, and ordering per key matters (partitions scale, keys preserve order).
- You build event-driven microservices, change data capture pipelines, clickstream, log or metrics pipelines, or stream processing on live data.
- You want a durable buffer between systems that run at different speeds.

Think twice, or choose something else, when:

- The caller needs an immediate answer. Use HTTP or gRPC, not a log.
- You have a small job queue that needs delays, priorities or per-message timeouts. A broker, a cloud queue or a database-backed queue fits better (Kafka share groups help with some queue needs, not with these).
- You need ad hoc queries and multi-row transactions. That is a database's job.
- Messages are huge blobs. Store them in object storage and send a reference.
- You need one strict global order of all events. A single partition caps throughput, so rethink the requirement.
- The volume is tiny, the team is small and nobody can operate a cluster. A managed service or a simpler tool may save you real money and sleep.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Kafka's own "use cases" page lists messaging, website activity tracking, metrics, log aggregation, stream processing, event sourcing and commit log. Its "Powered By" page mentions, for example, LinkedIn using Kafka for activity stream data and operational metrics, Netflix running a real-time monitoring and event-processing pipeline on it, and Uber treating it as a central part of its infrastructure. Treat such lists as inspiration, not as proof that Kafka suits your problem.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When would you not choose Kafka? When the interaction is request-response, when you need per-message features such as priorities or delays, when you need rich queries or transactions across records, when payloads are very large, or when the volume does not justify operating a cluster. In those cases an RPC call, a message broker or cloud queue, a database or object storage is usually the better fit.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- Queues share work between competing consumers; publish-subscribe broadcasts. Kafka's consumer groups do both.
- Brokers delete messages after acknowledgement and push them; Kafka keeps records, lets consumers pull, and lets them replay.
- Databases hold current state and answer queries; Kafka holds the history of changes. Use them together.
- Managed services trade portability for less operations work. Pulsar and Redpanda are real alternatives with different designs, and Kafka-protocol compatibility does not mean identical behaviour.

sections.title: What Kafka Guarantees (and What It Does Not)

blocks.text:
Before you trust a system with orders and payments, you need to know what it promises and under which conditions. This chapter states Kafka's guarantees in plain words. Each one comes with fine print, and later parts of the book explain the mechanics behind it.

### The guarantees

blocks.text:
Two of these deserve a closer look because they are easy to misread.

**Durability is about replication, not about forcing every write to disk.** By default Kafka does not flush each write to disk before it acknowledges it. It acknowledges once the in-sync replicas have the record (in the operating system's page cache) and relies on the other replicas surviving the failure of a single machine. The architecture part of the book discusses this choice. For you it means that the replication factor and `min.insync.replicas` are your durability settings, not an afterthought.

**Delivery is at least once unless you design otherwise.** Suppose `payment-service` reads `OrderCreated` at offset 41 of partition 2, charges the customer's card, and crashes before it commits offset 42. After the restart the same record is delivered again, and without protection the customer is charged twice. Kafka did nothing wrong: it preferred duplicates to loss. The fix is to make the consumer **idempotent**, for example by storing the payment id or event id and skipping events that were already handled. Kafka can also give exactly-once results for a read-process-write cycle that stays inside Kafka (transactions, covered later), but never for side effects in the outside world, such as a card charge or an email.

### What is not guaranteed

- **Global order.** There is no order between records in different partitions. If the order of two kinds of events matters, give them the same key so they share a partition.
- **Delivery to every consumer of a group.** Inside a group each record goes to one member. Use separate groups for separate applications that each need every record.
- **Exactly-once side effects.** See above: idempotent consumers are your responsibility.
- **Unlimited memory of the past.** Data older than the retention setting is deleted, whether or not anybody read it.
- **Safety with weak settings.** With `acks=0` or `acks=1`, or with a replication factor of 1, a broker failure can lose acknowledged data. The guarantees above describe a sensibly configured cluster.
- **Valid data.** Kafka stores bytes. It does not check that a value is valid JSON or that a field exists; schemas are enforced by clients and a schema registry, covered in the serialization part.
- **Hard real-time latency.** Latency is typically low, but there is no upper bound that you can promise to a customer.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not read "at least once" as "exactly once in practice". Duplicates are rare in a healthy system, which makes them dangerous: the code path that handles them is the least tested one. Design every consumer so that processing the same event twice produces the same result as processing it once, and test that path on purpose.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Does Kafka guarantee exactly-once delivery? Not by default. The default end-to-end behaviour is at least once. Kafka offers exactly-once semantics for the consume-transform-produce cycle inside Kafka by combining the idempotent producer, transactions and consumers that read only committed records (`isolation.level=read_committed`). Side effects outside Kafka still need idempotent consumers or a deduplication key.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- Order is guaranteed inside a partition only, so keys express your ordering requirements.
- Durability comes from replication: use `acks=all`, a replication factor of 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`.
- Delivery is at least once by default, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.
- Retention, not consumption, decides how long data stays. Kafka stores bytes and does not validate them.

*These are separate projects or products. Check their current status and licence before you adopt them.*

The official documentation says there are "a plethora of tools that integrate with Kafka outside the main distribution" and keeps a community list on the project wiki. Treat every third-party tool as a dependency: look at its release activity, its licence, and whether it supports Kafka 4.x before you build on it.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: When a problem sounds like a pipeline, look for a connector first. Copying rows from a database into Kafka, or topics into a search index, is almost never worth custom consumer code. Kafka Connect already handles offsets, retries, scaling and error routing. Write your own code for business logic, and use Connect for plumbing.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- Apache Kafka ships the clients, Kafka Streams, Kafka Connect, MirrorMaker 2 and the command-line tools.
- Schema registries, ksqlDB, Debezium, UIs, operators and managed services are separate projects: check licence, maintenance and Kafka 4.x support.
- Use Connect for data movement and Streams for processing before you write consumers by hand.

sections.title: A Short History and the Kafka 4.x Era

blocks.text:
### From LinkedIn to the Apache Software Foundation

Kafka was created at LinkedIn by a team that included Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao, to collect and distribute activity stream data and operational metrics. It was open-sourced in 2011 and became a top-level Apache project in

1. Several of its creators later founded Confluent, a company that builds

products around Kafka. The name is a reference to the writer Franz Kafka. Today Kafka is developed in the open under the Apache Software Foundation by contributors from many companies, and changes are discussed as **Kafka** **Improvement Proposals** (KIPs), each with a number such as KIP-500 or KIP-848.

### From ZooKeeper to KRaft

For most of its life Kafka stored its cluster metadata (topics, partitions, leaders, configuration) in Apache ZooKeeper, a separate coordination service. That meant running and securing two distributed systems, and the metadata design limited how many partitions a cluster could handle and how fast it recovered from a controller failure. **KIP-500**, "Replace ZooKeeper with a Self-Managed Metadata Quorum", proposed that Kafka manage its own metadata in an internal replicated log, using a Raft-based protocol that became known as **KRaft**.

The road took several years: KRaft arrived as early access in Kafka 2.8, was declared production-ready in Kafka 3.3, and ZooKeeper mode was deprecated in Kafka 3.5. Kafka 3.9 was the last release that could still run with ZooKeeper, and Kafka 4.0 removed it. Since then KRaft is the only mode, which is why this book never mentions ZooKeeper again, except when you meet it in older material.

### What each 4.x release added

rows: First release without ZooKeeper. The new consumer rebalance protocol (KIP-848) is generally available: broker side on by default, clients opt in with `group.protocol=consumer`. Share groups in early access (KIP-932). Brokers, Connect and tools need Java 17; clients and Streams need Java 11. Old protocol versions removed (KIP-896). Message formats v0 and v1, MirrorMaker 1 and `poll(long)` removed. Logging moves to Log4j 2
Share groups in preview. Streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071) in early access. Eligible leader replicas (ELR, KIP-966) enabled by default for new clusters

Share groups production-ready. Streams rebalance protocol production-ready for its core features. Dead-letter-queue support in Kafka Streams exception handlers (KIP-1034). RENEW acknowledgement for share consumers (KIP-1222). Java 25 support. Consistent command-line option names (KIP-1147)

Cordoning of brokers and log directories, so that no new partitions are placed there (KIP-1066). More configuration for share groups (KIP-1240). Partition size percentage metrics for storage monitoring (KIP-1257). Streams: a setting to remove stale state directories at startup (KIP-1259) and headers in state stores (KIP-1271). Follower fetch from a tiered offset (KIP-1023). The Scala wrapper for Kafka Streams is deprecated (KIP-1244)
blocks.caption: Highlights of the Kafka 4.x releases (each KIP number is the proposal you can look up).

blocks.text:
At the time of writing (October 2026) the supported lines are 4.3 (latest patch 4.3.1), 4.2 (4.2.2) and 4.1 (4.1.2). The book uses 4.3.1 for broker examples, and quotes defaults from the 4.2 documentation, which matches 4.3 unless stated.

### Versioning and compatibility

Kafka versions are written major.minor.patch. A minor release (4.2, 4.3) adds features and arrives every few months; the four feature releases above were spread over about fourteen months. Patch releases (4.3.1) fix bugs. Features and removals are announced first as **deprecations**: the 4.2 release notes, for example, say that the old command-line spellings and some other items "will be removed in Kafka 5.0", which tells you today what to avoid.

The compatibility rules you should know are these.

- **Clients and brokers.** Since Kafka 4.0, a broker accepts only clients that are version 2.1 or newer, and 4.x clients need brokers of version 2.1 or newer (KIP-896). Clients from the 3.x line are fully compatible with 4.x brokers, and clients between 2.1 and 2.8 work with limits.
- **Java.** Brokers, Connect and the tools need Java 17 or newer. The Java clients and Kafka Streams need Java 11 or newer. Java 8 support ended with 4.0.
- **Upgrades.** A rolling upgrade restarts brokers one at a time and is finished by raising the feature level with `kafka-features.sh`; metadata downgrades are not supported. The production part walks through it.

Where to look things up: the **downloads page** (`kafka.apache.org/downloads`) links the release notes of each version, the **blog** (`kafka.apache.org/blog`) has a readable announcement for every release, the **upgrade guide** in the documentation lists every behaviour change, and the **KIP pages** on the Apache wiki explain why a change was made.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Documentation is versioned. The documentation lives under a version-specific path, for example `kafka.apache.org/42/` for 4.2. When a setting or a behaviour surprises you, check the page that matches your broker version.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- Kafka began at LinkedIn, was open-sourced in 2011 and became an Apache top-level project in 2012.
- KIP-500 replaced ZooKeeper by KRaft: early access in 2.8, production-ready in 3.3, deprecated ZooKeeper in 3.5, removed in 4.0.
- 4.x brought the new rebalance protocol, share groups (production-ready in 4.2) and many operational improvements.
- Clients and brokers must be 2.1 or newer to interoperate with 4.x; brokers need Java 17, clients Java 11.

This book is built for a learner who has never used Kafka and wants three things at the end: a mental model that survives interview questions, the ability to build real applications, and enough operational sense to run a cluster without fear. The path below gets you there in the order in which the ideas depend on each other.

Each part answers one question. What is Kafka and when do I use it? How do I run it and poke at it? How does it work inside? How do I write a producer and a consumer in plain Java? How do I model and evolve data? How do I do all of that with Spring Boot? How do I handle failure in production code? How do I process streams and move data in and out? Which design patterns are proven? Where is Kafka used? How do I put it all together? How do I operate it? And finally, how do I revise for an interview?

### A four-week plan

The plan assumes about fifteen hours a week of reading and lab work. If you study part-time, stretch each week to two.

rows: Kafka fundamentals, the hands-on labs, the architecture and internals
You can explain partitions, offsets, consumer groups, replication and the in-sync replica set from memory, and you ran every lab
The Java producer and consumer, serialization and schemas
You wrote a producer and a consumer, chose acknowledgements and commit strategies on purpose, and evolved a schema safely
Spring Boot with Spring Kafka, errors, retries and testing, then Kafka Streams
A Spring service publishes and consumes events with retries and a dead-letter topic; a Streams topology aggregates page views
Kafka Connect and CDC, design patterns, use cases, one end-to-end project, production, the revision kit
You can design an outbox or saga flow, you built one project, and you can answer the interview questions
blocks.caption: A suggested four-week schedule. Do the labs, they are the point.

blocks.text:
In a hurry before an interview? Read the fundamentals and the architecture parts, the reliability chapters of the producer and consumer parts, the patterns part, and then work through the revision kit. Spring-first reader? Do the fundamentals and the hands-on labs, then jump to the Spring parts and come back to the Java clients when something confuses you.

### How the labs and listings work

- **Labs** are the amber banners. Each has a goal, numbered steps in dark terminal boxes, an explanation of what just happened, and a "try it yourself" exercise. Predict the output before you press Enter; the gap between your prediction and reality is where learning happens.
- **Terminal output** is typical output. Ids, offsets, timestamps and column spacing on your machine will differ.
- **Listings** use the package `com.shopstream` and the event names introduced in this book. Complete files include their imports; fragments say so.
- **Versions.** Broker examples use Kafka 4.3.1, plain Java uses `kafka-clients` 4.3.1, and the Spring examples take versions from Spring Boot 4.1.x and its Spring for Apache Kafka 4.1.x.

blocks.text: Kafka's tools are shell scripts. On Windows, use WSL 2 or run the tools inside the Docker container. A laptop with several gigabytes of free memory is enough for everything except the three-node cluster, which starts six JVMs; close other heavy applications when you run it.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Keep a learning log. After every chapter write three lines: what problem it solves, one thing that surprised you, and one question you cannot yet answer. Review the questions at the start of the next session. The interview boxes in each chapter are a ready-made quiz: cover the answer and say yours out loud first.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
What to remember from this chapter

- Study in dependency order: fundamentals, hands-on labs, internals, then the clients, then Spring, then Streams and Connect.
- Run every lab, and predict the output before you run it.
- Install a JDK 21, the Kafka 4.3.1 tarball, Docker with Compose and Maven before you start the hands-on part.
